rationale: B wins because its proof gates are sharper and its beats separate more cleanly. "A grocery marketplace built a $1B ad business out of 6,000 brands" asks the questions a real ad-trade reporter will ask before the founder embarrasses themselves; A's "What 6,000 Consumer Brands Buying Grocery Ads Reveals About Where CPG Money Is Moving" is useful but slides into the same retail-media lane with a little trend perfume. B still needs an editor's hand on overclaiming, but it gives the founder better press strategy.
gaps_in_A: "a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners" overstates the facts. The update says Instacart has 1,500+ retail banners and carts plan to expand; it does not say carts are expanding across that whole partner base.
"as digital attribution has gotten harder" is outside the supplied update. Maybe true, maybe not; in this exercise it is decoration pretending to be context.

"With $1B in Ad Revenue and 6,000 Brands" and "What 6,000 Consumer Brands Buying Grocery Ads" are too close. The second angle needs a genuinely different proof base, or it should be folded into the retail-media angle.
A asks for revenue mix and buyer proof, but misses the first finance question: how the "$1B annual run rate" is calculated. A reporter will ask that before they ask for the grand theory.
gaps_in_B: "Instacart's delivery growth has stalled" is too strong. The update says growth slowed to single digits; that is not the same as stalled, unless the number is near zero.
"slowing core, accelerating adjacency" invents acceleration. The facts show a $1B ad run rate, not the ad business's growth rate.
"Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it" turns partnerships into a make-versus-buy thesis the update does not prove. Good question, overcooked headline.

"ads on top" in the retailer-strategy angle risks implying an integrated grocery tech stack the facts do not establish. B is disciplined elsewhere about not claiming cart ads; it should apply the same discipline here.
